explanations.explanation: Clean is exactly what he asks for, friend. The man says, “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” (Mark 1:40) He doesn't ask for a little help or a nicer week. He asks for the whole thing, and he asks it on his knees.
Wise sounds nice, but that's not what he's after. He says, “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” (Mark 1:40) A man living with leprosy wants one thing, and it isn't a bigger brain.

I get the guess, because it takes guts to drop to your knees in front of a crowd. But brave isn't what he asks for. He says, “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” (Mark 1:40) Clean is the word he picks.
That's it, baker. “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” (Mark 1:40) He has no doubt about what Jesus can do. The "if" is about whether Jesus will. I think that's a humble way to ask.

Close in spirit, but those aren't his words. He says, “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” (Mark 1:40) The "if" lands on Jesus' willingness, not on how worthy the man is. The text doesn't have him say a word about himself there.
Nope, no faith meter on this one. The man says, “If You are willing, You can make me clean.” (Mark 1:40) His "if" points at Jesus being willing. He never says a thing about how much faith he's got.

True! Mark says, “Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man.” (Mark 1:41) Under the Law, a leper had to live alone (Leviticus 13:46). And Jesus reaches right out and touches him. I think that touch meant a lot.

It's actually true, friend. The text says, “Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man.” (Mark 1:41) A leper was supposed to live alone, outside the camp (Leviticus 13:46). Yet Jesus reaches out His hand to him.
True, and there's no waiting around. “And immediately the leprosy left him, and the man was cleansed.” (Mark 1:42) No second visit, no follow-up appointment. Jesus speaks and it's done.
It's actually true, baker. Mark says, “And immediately the leprosy left him, and the man was cleansed.” (Mark 1:42) The word is immediately. Nothing slow or gradual about it.
Tell is the word. Jesus says, “See that you don't tell anyone.” (Mark 1:44) That's a pretty big ask when you've just been healed. I'd be bursting like a cookie box with no lid.
Touch is a fun guess, since Jesus just touched him. But the warning is, “See that you don’t tell anyone.” (Mark 1:44) It's about telling, not touching.
Not visit, friend. The warning is, “See that you don’t tell anyone.” (Mark 1:44) Jesus does send him to one place, the priest, but the stern warning is about keeping quiet.
The priest, yes. Jesus says, “But go, show yourself to the priest…” (Mark 1:44) So the man isn't told to just keep quiet and wander off. He's given a place to go.
Scribes are a good guess, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “But go, show yourself to the priest…” (Mark 1:44) The priest is the one he's sent to.
Not the elders, baker. Jesus says, “But go, show yourself to the priest…” (Mark 1:44) That's the one on the list, and he's the only one named in this passage.
That's the one. Jesus says to present the offering Moses prescribed “…as a testimony to them.” (Mark 1:44) Mark doesn't say more about who "them" is. So I'll leave it right there.
That's not what Jesus says. He says to present the offering Moses prescribed “…as a testimony to them.” (Mark 1:44) The word He uses is testimony. Nothing about payment shows up in this verse.
Good heart, but no. Jesus says the offering is “…as a testimony to them.” (Mark 1:44) The text doesn't call it a gift for anybody. Testimony is the word.

Ooh, so close to a good plan, but no. Mark says, “But the man went out and openly began to proclaim and spread the news.” (Mark 1:45) Jesus said not to tell anyone, and this man tells everybody. That's the opposite of keeping it to himself.
False is right, baker. “But the man went out and openly began to proclaim and spread the news.” (Mark 1:45) Jesus told him not to tell anyone. He spread the news anyway, and he did it openly.

explanations.answer: He can't enter a town in plain view
explanations.explanation: Right. Mark says, “Consequently, Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view…” (Mark 1:45) The news travels, and it changes where Jesus can go. Plain view is out.

explanations.answer: He has to send the crowds away
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says, “Consequently, Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view…” (Mark 1:45) The change is about where He can go. No crowds get sent away in this passage.

explanations.answer: He has to cross the sea by boat
explanations.explanation: No boat in this passage, friend. Mark says, “Consequently, Jesus could no longer enter a town in plain view…” (Mark 1:45) The change is that He can't go into towns openly. The sea doesn't come up.

explanations.answer: People come to Him from every quarter
explanations.explanation: You got it. “Yet people came to Him from every quarter.” (Mark 1:45) Jesus is out in solitary places, and folks still find Him. Even the quiet spots get busy!

explanations.answer: His disciples go back to fishing
explanations.explanation: Not in this passage, baker. It says, “Yet people came to Him from every quarter.” (Mark 1:45) Nobody goes back to fishing here. The people are coming to Jesus.

explanations.answer: The priests come out to question Him
explanations.explanation: Not here. The text says, “Yet people came to Him from every quarter.” (Mark 1:45) Mark doesn't mention priests coming out to Him. It's people, from every direction.
